faq.a: A negative ANA makes lupus unlikely (NPV ≈ 99 %) but very rare ANA‑negative lupus exists; clinical judgment remains essential.
faq.q: Can a negative ANA rule out lupus?

faq.a: ANA is highly sensitive but not specific; many diseases and healthy people can be positive, so disease‑specific antibodies and clinical criteria are required.
faq.q: Why is ANA screening not sufficient for diagnosis?

faq.a: Use an ELISA ANA test, acknowledging lower sensitivity; if still negative but suspicion is high, send a sample to a reference lab.
faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot perform IIF ANA?

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with malar rash, arthralgia and proteinuria. ANA is 1:1280. – Explain why ANA alone does not confirm SLE and which next test you would order.
A patient on long‑term hydralazine develops a positive ANA but no symptoms. – Discuss management and whether to stop the drug.
In a malaria‑endemic region, a febrile patient has a low‑titre ANA (1:40). – How do you differentiate infection‑related positivity from early autoimmune disease?
You receive an ANA report with a titre of 1:80 from a lab that uses a different cut‑off. – How do you interpret this result in your clinical context?
A patient with known SLE develops rising anti‑dsDNA titres and falling complement. – What does this indicate and what immediate treatment steps are indicated?
During a routine check, a 65‑year‑old asymptomatic man has ANA 1:40. – What counseling would you give regarding future risk?
A rural clinic lacks HEp‑2 IIF; only ELISA is available. – How would you use ELISA results to guide further work‑up?
Explain why hydroxychloroquine is preferred as first‑line therapy in ANA‑positive SLE despite the presence of renal disease.
ai.title: Antinuclear Antibodies (ANA) in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: ANA are auto‑antibodies directed against nuclear components. They are a screening tool for systemic autoimmune disease, especially SLE, but must be interpreted in context and with confirmatory tests.

b: Screening test – high sensitivity, low specificity
Positive in >95 % of active systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Negative test makes SLE unlikely (NPV ≈ 99 %)
sections.p: ANA are immunoglobulins that bind to cellular nuclear antigens. The test is performed by indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) on HEp‑2 cells; a positive result indicates the presence of any nuclear‑directed auto‑antibody, not a specific disease.

b: Low titre (≤1:40) – often benign or false‑positive
Intermediate (1:80–1:320) – warrants further testing if clinical suspicion exists
High (≥1:640) – strong association with systemic autoimmunity
sections.p: ANA titres are reported as a dilution (e.g., 1:80, 1:320). Higher titres correlate with higher likelihood of autoimmune disease but do not grade severity. Disease activity is assessed with disease‑specific antibodies (e.g., anti‑dsDNA) and clinical indices.

b: Systemic lupus erythematosus – primary cause of high‑titre ANA
Mixed connective tissue disease, Sjögren’s syndrome, systemic sclerosis
Chronic infections prevalent locally – HIV, hepatitis B/C, tuberculosis, malaria (occasionally produce low‑titre ANA)
Silicosis and other occupational lung diseases
Drug‑induced autoimmunity – procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid
sections.p: ANA can arise from many conditions; the most common in low‑resource settings are:

b: Malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers (SLE)
Raynaud’s phenomenon, skin thickening (systemic sclerosis)
Dry eyes/mouth, parotid enlargement (Sjögren’s)
Arthralgia, myalgia, unexplained fever
sections.p: Patients are identified because of multisystem complaints that raise suspicion for autoimmune disease.

t.b: Is there any nuclear‑directed auto‑antibody? – Positive suggests autoimmune disease; if unavailable, use ELISA as a substitute but note lower sensitivity.
Is SLE likely and active? – Positive, especially at high titre, supports SLE and correlates with renal activity.
Which specific connective‑tissue disease? – Identifies antibodies such as anti‑RNP, anti‑SSA/SSB, anti‑Scl‑70.

t.a: Complete blood count, renal & liver function, urinalysis
t.b: What organ involvement exists? – Detects cytopenias, proteinuria, transaminitis that guide urgency.

b: Lupus nephritis – rapid rise in proteinuria or creatinine
Neuropsychiatric lupus – new seizures, psychosis, severe headache
Pulmonary hemorrhage or severe vasculitis
sections.p: A positive ANA alone is not an emergency, but associated organ disease can be life‑threatening.

b: SLE – start hydroxychloroquine (disease‑modifying, safe in most settings) and steroids for organ involvement.
Severe organ disease – add mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide; avoid drugs with high hepatotoxicity if liver disease co‑exists.
Drug‑induced ANA – discontinue offending agent; monitor for resolution.
sections.p: Treat the underlying autoimmune disease; ANA results guide further testing rather than therapy.

b: Check anti‑dsDNA and complement every 3–6 months in active SLE.
Educate patients on sun protection, infection prophylaxis, and medication adherence.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus in immunosuppressed patients.
sections.p: Serial disease‑specific antibodies (anti‑dsDNA) and clinical review are more useful than repeat ANA.

b: Chronic infections (HIV, hepatitis C) – low‑titre ANA, no systemic autoimmunity
Age‑related positivity – titres ≤1:40 in healthy elderly
Rheumatoid factor positivity – different target (Fc portion of IgG)
sections.p: Conditions that produce a positive ANA but are not autoimmune:

b: Low‑titre ANA in isolation – may be false‑positive; always correlate with clinical picture.
Laboratory variability – different labs use different cut‑offs; request the lab’s reference range.
ANA‑negative SLE – rare; rely on clinical criteria and specific antibodies.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of renal failure or heavy proteinuria
Severe unexplained fever with organ dysfunction
